entities.summary: Jean de Corbeil, Seigneur of Grez-sur-Loing, was a Marshal of France. He played a crucial role in the French struggle for independence against the English in the late 13th century, leading the French forces to victory at the Battle of Crécy in 1346. De Corbeil's military prowess and strategic thinking earned him recognition from King Philip VI, who appointed him as the commander of the French army in the Hundred Years' War. As a Marshal, de Corbeil was responsible for overseeing the construction of fortifications and roads in France, contributing significantly to the country's military preparedness. His legacy continued to shape French military strategy for centuries to come. The 14th-century historian Jean Froissart often referred to de Corbeil as a 'great captain' of the French army, cementing his reputation as one of the most skilled military leaders of his era. The Battle of Crécy, where de Corbeil led the French to victory, remains a pivotal moment in the Hundred Years' War, showcasing the effectiveness of the longbowmen and the French use of infantry tactics. De Corbeil's influence on French military history can be seen in the development of the 'French way of war,' which emphasized the use of infantry and the deployment of troops in a defensive position. Despite the passage of time, de Corbeil's name continues to be invoked by historians and military strategists alike, testifying to his enduring impact on the art of war.
